name: Rafael Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead construction crew for one of the big private power companies, out on the edge of the city where they're building new housing estates as fast as they can pour concrete. We set poles, run new lines, hook up transformers for streets that were fields last spring. I'm second year, still the apprentice, so I dig, I rig, I haul, and I climb when Hector, our lead, says I can.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twelve years in the army, in signals, then eight years as a security guard at the shopping centre, which nearly killed me with boredom. A veterans' apprenticeship came up at 41 and I took it, because I wanted to work with my hands and bring home a proper wage for Teresa and the kids. What wears me out is being the old new guy, I'm slower than the young ones and my shoulders ache, but I like the discipline of it, it feels like the army without anybody shooting at you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can get back to real work. At the depot it'd be a five-minute laugh at break. I'm not a big poster, maybe I'd share something funny in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan holds, two more years, get my ticket, journeyman wage. The estates keep getting built and somebody has to power them. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like now. I'd still use the AI thing now and then for writing emails to the office, because I'm no good with words, and Teresa uses it for her bookkeeping. We'd keep saving, we've got about three months of bills, and I'd like to put a bit toward Gabriel's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI for emails. How did you get into that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teresa showed me after she started using it for her clients' accounts. I'd write a message to the office that sounded like a sergeant shouting, she'd run it through and it came out polite. Now I do it myself, but only once she'd shown me it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, if anything, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates and the mortgage, same as everyone. And whether the building slows down, because if they stop building estates, our crew shrinks. That's the real risk for me, not computers.

S0.say: Good, now people can get back to real work. It'd be a five-minute laugh at break and maybe a funny post in the family group chat.
S0.think: It means my plan holds: two more years, my ticket, then a journeyman wage. The estates keep getting built and somebody has to power them, and that's me.
S0.do: Keeps going as now, using AI now and then to make his emails to the office sound polite. Keeps saving on top of about three months of bills and starts putting a little toward his son's future.
S0.quote: I'd write a message to the office that sounded like a sergeant shouting, she'd run it through and it came out polite.
S0.fieldNote: Ex-army discipline runs through how he talks about work and planning. He only picked up AI after his wife showed him it worked, which fits his proven-first approach. His real risk, he says, is a slowdown in house building, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, that's how it's always been. In the army they changed the radios on us three times and you learned the new one or you were useless. I'd tell the young guys the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we're fine for a good while on the construction side. Building new lines on new estates is messy, every site's different, the ground's different. The bit that might go is the office side, the planning and the inspections, and that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the company brings in, and once the first crews were using it and it worked, I'd get trained on it. I'd use the AI stuff a bit more for my apprenticeship study. And I'd keep putting money by as normal, no big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of keeping my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it did cost jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the companies, they've got to stay competitive, that's business. I'd blame anyone who refuses to learn and then wants someone else to pay for them. And maybe the schools for not teaching kids trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gabriel, who's 13?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade, get your hands dirty, and learn the new tools too. Same as I'd tell any young man. Work is what keeps a person straight.

S1.say: Adapt or get left behind, that's how it's always been. In the army they changed the radios on us three times and you learned the new one or you were useless.
S1.think: I think construction work is fine for a good while, because every new estate is messy and different. The planning and inspections might go, but that's not me.
S1.do: Watches what the company brings in and gets trained once the first crews show it works. Uses AI a bit more for his apprenticeship study and keeps saving as normal.
S1.feel: Calm, mostly, while keeping his eyes open.
S1.quote: In the army they changed the radios on us three times and you learned the new one or you were useless.
S1.fieldNote: He frames change as a discipline issue: you learn the new kit or you're useless. He doesn't blame companies for staying competitive and is sharper on people who refuse to learn. He waits for proof from other crews before training, in line with his steady approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, and people are going to need to pull together, families, churches, neighbourhoods. I wouldn't be one for marching about it. I'd say keep calm and look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be in real trouble. If robots can climb and string lines, they'll be on the new estates first, because it's all new kit on clear ground, perfect for them. And I'm the second-year apprentice, so I'd be first out, two years before I ever got my ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no holiday, the old car keeps going, the kids' extras on hold. I'd pick up weekend work, security shifts maybe, or handyman jobs around the parish, while there's still demand. And Teresa and I would lean on her parents if it came to it, they've offered before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken, honestly. I haven't felt that since my last tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not for handouts. If the government offered support in this one, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if I'd worked for it, like unemployment I've paid into. I wouldn't feel right taking something for nothing. But I won't let my kids go short for pride either, I'll say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the savings and get a second income going, that's it. Two years isn't long enough to train for anything that'd still be there. I'd go back to basics, like the army taught me.

S2.say: This is a shock, and people will need to pull together: families, churches, neighbourhoods. I wouldn't march about it, I'd say keep calm and look after your own.
S2.think: I'd be in real trouble, because new estates on clear ground are perfect for robots and I'm the second-year apprentice. I'd be first out, two years before I ever got my ticket.
S2.do: Cuts back hard at once on holidays, car and children's extras, and picks up weekend security or handyman work around the parish. Leans on his wife's parents if needed and takes support he has paid into, like unemployment insurance.
S2.feel: Shaken, in a way he hasn't felt since his last army tour.
S2.quote: I'd take it if I'd worked for it, like unemployment I've paid into. I wouldn't feel right taking something for nothing.
S2.fieldNote: He spotted that his work, new lines on clear ground, might be among the first that robots could do. His instinct is family, parish and a second job, and he'd accept only support he has earned. Pride and providing for his children pull against each other, and he named it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so get ready. Companies should be putting on apprenticeships for the new jobs now. I'd say it at church and at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be qualified and have three years as a journeyman. That's a better wage and some savings behind me. But I'd still be one of the newer ones when it hits, so I'd still be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my ticket, then put the extra journeyman money into savings, aiming for six months. I'd start a small handyman business on Saturdays around year two, so there's something else coming in. And once I saw the first robot crews working, I'd get on whatever training they offered to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a soldier's kind of anxious, I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gabriel now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Different from before. I'd still say learn to work with your hands, but also learn how the machines think. He'd be 18 by then, so it really matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out after Mass on Sundays, which is our treat. Then the second car. I'd keep Lucia's dance, she lives for it.

S3.say: There's time to get ready, so get ready. Companies should be putting on apprenticeships for the new jobs now.
S3.think: In five years I'd be qualified with three years as a journeyman, which means a better wage and some savings. But I'd still be one of the newer ones when it hits, so I'd still be worried.
S3.do: Finishes his ticket and puts the extra journeyman wage into savings, aiming for six months. Starts a Saturday handyman business around year two, and trains to run robot crews once he sees the first ones working.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a soldier's kind of anxious, with a plan.
S3.quote: Anxious, but it's a soldier's kind of anxious, I'd have a plan.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him room for a structured plan: qualify, save, side business, then training once others have proven it. His advice to his son shifts to include understanding machines. Small family treats like Sunday lunch after Mass are the first things he'd cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. Nobody should need a handout if they've been given a decade's notice. I'd say that, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53 and a journeyman for eight years, maybe leading a crew like Hector. That's a good place to be. When it lands I'd expect to be one of the ones they keep to oversee things, at least for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, qualify, and be the best journeyman I can. In years four or five, once I see what's working, get trained on the robot side. And put some savings into an index fund every month, slowly, for when the kids go to college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between a retreat and a march. With two years I'm scrambling. With ten I can plan it like an operation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody should need a handout with a decade's notice. What about someone like Hector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hector's 60, so he'd be retired, God willing. But yes, there'll be people who can't make the jump, and their families and churches should be the first ones there. I suppose the government too, if it's done right, as a last resort.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. Nobody should need a handout after a decade's notice.
S4.think: In ten years I'd be 53, a journeyman for eight years and maybe leading a crew like Hector. When it lands I'd expect to be kept on to oversee things, at least for a few years.
S4.do: Keeps going, qualifies and works to be the best journeyman he can. Trains on the robot side in years four or five once he sees what works, and puts a little into an index fund every month for his children's college.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly fine.
S4.quote: It's the difference between a retreat and a march.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets him treat the change like a planned operation, with military language throughout. He holds a firm line against handouts but softened when asked about people who can't make the jump. Family and church come first in his idea of help, government last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be thrown out before I'd even finished my apprenticeship, at 45, with two kids and a mortgage. What would help is the companies keeping apprenticeships going and training their own people for the new jobs, and letting people earn their way through it rather than paying them to sit at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. A man needs to bring something home. If the robots do everything, I worry more about what happens to men like me sitting at home than I do about the money.

headlineQuote: If the robots do everything, I worry more about what happens to men like me sitting at home than I do about the money.
portrait: Rafael Baker is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice on an overhead construction crew for a private power company, wiring new housing estates on the edge of a city. He served twelve years in army signals and eight as a security guard before a veterans' apprenticeship, and lives with his wife Teresa, a part-time bookkeeper, their two children and a mortgage. He is traditional, believes in work over handouts, and picks up technology once he's seen it work. He is calm through a plateau and steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years because it would end his apprenticeship early, and plans methodically when given five or ten years. His deepest worry is the loss of pride and purpose, not just income.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be thrown out before finishing his apprenticeship, at 45 with two children and a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping apprenticeships going and training their own people for new jobs, so people can earn their way through rather than being paid to stay home.
